cues.text: Chosen to Serve
The Acts of the Apostles introduces Stephen amid genuine tension within the young Jerusalem Church.
Greek-speaking widows were being overlooked in the daily distribution of food.

Unwilling to neglect the ministry of the Word for administration, the Apostles asked the community to select seven men "of good repute, full of the Spirit and of wisdom" to oversee this charitable work.
Stephen, described as "a man full of faith and of the Holy Spirit," was the first named among these seven.
Though his ministry began by ensuring the poor were fairly fed, it quickly expanded.
Scripture tells us he was also "full of grace and power," performing great wonders and signs among the people.

We see here, at the very root of the diaconate, a truth the Church has never forgotten: that service to the poor and proclamation of the Gospel are never rivals, but flow from one and the same Spirit.
A Wisdom No One Could Resist

Stephen's preaching brought him into direct confrontation with members of a Hellenistic Jewish synagogue, who disputed with him but found themselves, Scripture records with striking simplicity, unable to withstand the wisdom and the Spirit with which he spoke.
Unable to defeat him in honest argument, his opponents resorted to procuring false witnesses.
They accused him of speaking blasphemous words against Moses and against the Temple.
These charges brought Stephen before the Sanhedrin, the same council that had recently condemned Jesus himself, on trumped-up accusations he had never actually made.
A Face Like an Angel's
As Stephen stood before his accusers, Scripture records a striking detail.
All who sat in the council, gazing at him, saw that his face was like the face of an angel.
This serenity amid mortal danger already anticipated the extraordinary courage of his coming defense.
Given the opportunity to answer the charges against him, Stephen instead delivered a sweeping recounting of Israel's entire salvation history.

It ran from Abraham through Moses to Solomon's Temple, building toward a climax that turned the accusation back upon his own judges: that they, like their ancestors, had always resisted the Holy Spirit.
They had now become the betrayers and murderers of the Righteous One whose coming the prophets had foretold.
"I See the Heavens Opened"
Stephen's unflinching accusation enraged the council, but rather than retreat, he pressed further still.
Gazing intently into heaven, he declared that he saw the glory of God, and Jesus standing at the right hand of the Father—a vision his furious listeners took as the final, unbearable blasphemy.
Covering their ears, the crowd rushed upon him with one accord, dragged him outside the city walls, and began to stone him.
Scripture notably records them laying their cloaks at the feet of a young man named Saul — the same Saul who would later, as Paul, become the Church's greatest missionary.
By his own later admission, he was present and complicit at the very death of the man whose faith he would one day spend his own life proclaiming.
A Death That Echoed Christ's Own
As the stones fell upon him, Stephen prayed two final petitions that deliberately echo Christ’s words upon the cross: first, Lord Jesus, receive my spirit .
Then, falling to his knees, he prayed, Lord, do not hold this sin against them — a prayer of forgiveness offered, quite literally, for the very people killing him, before he fell asleep in death.

We are given, in this one scene, a pattern that many Christian martyrs after him would seek to follow: a life poured out not in bitterness but in imitation of the Lord who had first forgiven from his own cross.
Legacy
Stephen's martyrdom marks a decisive turning point in the Acts of the Apostles, triggering a wider persecution.
This scattered the Jerusalem Christians throughout Judea and Samaria, unexpectedly accelerating the Gospel's spread far beyond the city where it had begun.
Honored ever since as the protomartyr , the first Christian to shed his blood for the faith, Stephen forgave his own killers even as they took his life.
His willingness remains one of the clearest, most immediate imitations of Christ's own passion in the whole of the New Testament.
This witness continues to teach every believer that forgiveness offered in the very hour of greatest injury is not weakness, but the fullest measure of a heart conformed to Christ.
